abstract: A compound that has not been made has no diffraction data to refine against. A model of electron density that is to be used in drug design must therefore be transferable: the same numbers for every protein and every ligand, nothing fitted per structure. The independent-atom model (IAM) is transferable, but it places no density in bonds and lets no atom respond to its surroundings. We set out to add both, explicitly and with few parameters, and tested each step on every Protein Data Bank X-ray entry with structure factors at 1.0 Angstrom or better (2,006 entries; 650 proteins never seen in training). Four things were learnt on the way. The benchmark itself had to be corrected first: in models deposited without hydrogen atoms, placing riding hydrogens lowers the R of the IAM by 0.0093 in 315 of 316 proteins, and about four fifths of what a transferable multipole model appeared to gain on them was the missing hydrogens. With hydrogens placed on every model, a layer that names each bond and contact, gives it one charge and one width and takes that charge from the valence shells of its atoms (the Complete Electron-cloud Layer, CEL) lowers R in 611 of 650 proteins, but by only 0.0007. Most of what the IAM leaves out is centred on the atoms and set by their surroundings. A neighbourhood field of 3,055 parameters, computed by matrix products from the types and distances of all atoms within 8 Angstrom, lowers R three times more than the bond layer, and the two together (3,214 parameters) are better than the multipole (4,768) in 545 of 650 proteins. And a bond has to be named by its chemical environment: with one class per pair of elements the C-N bond came out negative; with 25 classes defined beforehand the peptide bond is positive, the carbon skeleton carries 0.04 to 0.12 electrons per bond in a chemical order, and the layer is better on 602 of 650 unseen proteins. Read inversely, the bonds of the main chain stand out of the density in more than four proteins of five, and the polar bonds of ligands, which read below empty points in the density left by independent atoms, are restored by the field predicted from the surroundings, with its factor calibrated on ligand bonds against the per-atom solution. A per-atom solution of the same radial form lowers R by 0.017 on the reflections it is fitted to, but by about 0.002 on reflections held out of the fit, which is the size of what the field predicted from distances already delivers: the spherical form is close to what the data support, and the next gain has to come from direction. The bonds respond to their surroundings as well, but as a secondary effect: freed bond by bond and tested on held-out reflections, the charge of a bond changes by about 0.06 electron and gives one tenth of the gain of the atoms, and no shift of the bond charge is supported by the data.
